blocks.content: The last topic in this module was flow control, and it solved a very specific problem: a fast sender overwhelming one particular slow receiver. TCP fixed that with the receive window, a number the receiver constantly reports back to say exactly how much more data it can currently accept. That mechanism is entirely local. It only ever involves the two endpoints of a single connection talking to each other.

Congestion control is a genuinely different problem, and it closes out this Transport Layer module. Instead of protecting one receiver from one sender, it protects the network itself, the routers and links sitting in between, from being overwhelmed by the combined traffic of potentially thousands of completely unrelated connections, all sharing that same physical infrastructure at the exact same moment.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069770-744126189.png
1. A Different Problem From Flow Control
blocks.text: 1. A Different Problem From Flow Control

blocks.content: It helps to be precise about the difference, because the two ideas get confused constantly, even by people who already understand both individually. Flow control asks one question: is this particular receiver keeping up with this particular sender? Nothing about that question involves any other connection anywhere else on the network.

Congestion control asks a completely different question: is the network itself, the shared routers and links this connection happens to be passing through right now, able to handle everything currently being thrown at it? Your connection might have a receiver that is perfectly fast and ready for more data, and still need to slow down, because a router three hops away is being hammered by hundreds of other connections that have nothing to do with you.

That is the core distinction to hold onto for the rest of this topic. Flow control is local, a private conversation between two endpoints. Congestion control is about a shared, public resource that no single connection owns or controls, and every connection has to behave responsibly around it.

blocks.title: One receiver versus one network
blocks.content: Flow control protects a receiver that TCP already knows by name, the exact other end of this one connection. Congestion control protects a network that TCP never gets to see directly, shared with an unknown, constantly changing number of other connections it will never even know exist.
2. Why Network Congestion Is a Real, Dangerous Problem
blocks.text: 2. Why Network Congestion Is a Real, Dangerous Problem

blocks.content: Every router and every link has a real, physical ceiling on how much data it can forward per second. That capacity is not negotiable and not infinite. When the total traffic arriving at a router adds up to more than it can actually push out the other side, the extra data has to go somewhere, so it waits in a queue.

Queues help absorb short bursts, but they are not magic. If traffic keeps arriving faster than it can leave, the queue keeps filling, and once it is completely full, the router has no choice left. It starts dropping packets it simply has nowhere to put.

Here is the genuinely dangerous part. Those dropped packets do not just vanish quietly. TCP's reliability mechanism notices the missing data and retransmits it, exactly as it is designed to do. But that retransmission is brand new traffic, added right back onto a link that was already too busy to cope in the first place. Left unchecked, this becomes a vicious cycle: congestion causes drops, drops cause retransmissions, and retransmissions make the congestion worse.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069772-122502950.png
blocks.alt: Why Network Congestion Is a Real, Dangerous Problem

blocks.title: Congestion feeds on itself
blocks.content: This is what makes congestion different from ordinary slowness. A slow link is just slow. A congested link, left alone, can spiral into forwarding less and less useful data over time, because more and more of its capacity gets consumed by retransmissions of data it already tried and failed to deliver.
3. The Congestion Window: A Second, Different Limit
blocks.text: 3. The Congestion Window: A Second, Different Limit

blocks.content: To defend against this, TCP gives every sender a second number to track, completely separate from the receive window you already met. This one is called the congestion window, and it represents the sender's own running estimate of how much data the network, not the receiver, can currently handle without falling over.

The contrast with the receive window is exactly the point. The receive window is a number the receiver explicitly reports, based on its own buffer space. The congestion window is a number the sender works out for itself, based on how the network has been behaving recently, since no router along the way ever directly tells a TCP sender how busy it is.

TCP combines both numbers with a simple rule: the actual amount of data allowed in flight at any moment is whichever of the two windows is smaller right now. If the receiver is slow, the receive window wins and caps things. If the network is struggling, the congestion window wins instead. Either limit can be the one holding the sender back, and TCP always obeys the more restrictive one.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069772-434716440.png
blocks.alt: The Congestion Window: A Second, Different Limit

4. Ramping Up: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
blocks.text: 4. Ramping Up: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance

blocks.content: A brand new TCP connection has no idea how much capacity the network can actually give it, so it deliberately does not guess big. It begins in a phase called slow start, sending with a small congestion window and watching closely for acknowledgments confirming that data is actually arriving safely.

Every batch of successful acknowledgments lets the sender grow its congestion window and send a bit more next time. Because this growth compounds round after round, the window ramps up quickly at first, cautious at the very start, but picking up real speed once it is clear the network can handle it.

That fast ramp cannot continue forever, and TCP knows it. Once the congestion window grows past a certain threshold, TCP switches into a second, more careful phase called congestion avoidance. Growth does not stop, but it slows down considerably, adding only a small amount per round trip instead of compounding.

Think of it as TCP getting more cautious the closer it gets to the edge of what the network can handle. Early on, when a lost packet is unlikely and there is clearly room to spare, it is safe to grow fast. Later, once the window is large and getting close to the point where loss becomes likely, TCP deliberately eases off and probes the remaining capacity more gently.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069772-841785032.png
blocks.alt: Ramping Up: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance

blocks.content: 5. Reacting to Loss: The Emergency Brake
blocks.text: 5. Reacting to Loss: The Emergency Brake

blocks.content: Eventually, on almost every real connection, a packet does get lost. Maybe the congestion window finally grew past what the network could actually sustain, or maybe some unrelated burst of traffic filled a queue at exactly the wrong moment. Either way, TCP has to notice, and it does, through the same retransmission mechanism you met in the reliability topic.

TCP treats a detected loss as a strong, reliable signal that the network is congested right now, at this exact moment, whatever the actual cause turned out to be. It does not wait around to investigate further. It reacts immediately by shrinking the congestion window dramatically, cutting the amount of data it is willing to have in flight.

After that sharp cut, TCP does not just sit at the smaller window either. It begins the careful ramp up process again, slow start and then congestion avoidance, rebuilding its estimate of the network's capacity from a safer starting point. This growth, hit a limit, back off, grow again cycle is not a one time event. It repeats for the entire lifetime of a long running connection.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069773-769583880.png
blocks.alt: Reacting to Loss: The Emergency Brake

blocks.content: 6. The Sawtooth Pattern

Zoom out and watch a single TCP connection's congestion window over its entire lifetime, and a very distinctive shape appears. It climbs, sometimes quickly during slow start and then more gently during congestion avoidance, until a loss event cuts it sharply back down. Then it climbs again, and gets cut again, over and over.

This is exactly the sawtooth pattern that TCP throughput is famous for, and it is not a flaw or a bug. It is the visible signature of TCP constantly, deliberately probing for exactly how much the network can give it right now, backing off the moment it finds the edge, and trying again. The window is never allowed to sit still and grow unchecked forever.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437069773-250145831.png

blocks.title: Why the shape matters, not just the number
blocks.content: A single snapshot of the congestion window tells you almost nothing on its own. The sawtooth shape over time is what tells you TCP is actually working correctly, continuously adjusting itself to match a network whose real capacity is never directly announced to it.
7. Merging Onto a Highway: Why Cooperation Works
blocks.text: 7. Merging Onto a Highway: Why Cooperation Works

blocks.content: Picture a busy highway on ramp during rush hour. If every driver floors it the instant they see the smallest gap, cars pile in faster than the road can actually absorb them, and the whole highway locks into a jam where everyone, including the aggressive drivers, ends up crawling along far slower than if they had just waited their turn.

Now picture the alternative. Drivers merge carefully, watch for brake lights ahead, and ease off the moment traffic starts bunching up. Nobody is being purely selfless, they are just avoiding getting stuck in a jam they can see coming. And counterintuitively, that cautious, watchful behavior is exactly what keeps the whole highway moving faster overall.

Congestion control is every single TCP connection behaving like that cautious, cooperative driver. Nobody forces any individual connection to back off when it detects loss, it simply does, because that is what the protocol is designed to do, on every device, in every operating system, by default.

This matters enormously at the scale of the actual internet, which is shared right now by billions of simultaneous connections that have absolutely no coordination with each other. That shared infrastructure keeps working, mostly staying fast and responsive, specifically because TCP endpoints do not selfishly grab every bit of bandwidth they possibly could. They back off cooperatively, and the network survives its own popularity as a direct result.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437214902-168216946.png
blocks.alt: Merging Onto a Highway: Why Cooperation Works

blocks.content: /engineering/library/cn/images/1785437214904-198186336.png
blocks.alt: Merging Onto a Highway: Why Cooperation Works

blocks.title: This was learned the hard way
blocks.content: In the mid nineteen eighties, the early internet actually suffered a period researchers now call congestion collapse, where growing traffic caused real throughput to crash instead of grow. TCP's congestion control mechanisms exist largely because of that painful lesson.
8. Flow Control and Congestion Control, Side by Side
blocks.text: 8. Flow Control and Congestion Control, Side by Side

blocks.content: You have now seen both mechanisms in full, so it is worth putting them directly next to each other one final time, because keeping this distinction sharp is genuinely one of the most useful things to take away from this entire module.

Notice that both mechanisms end up doing the same physical thing, limiting how much data the sender puts in flight, which is exactly why they get confused so easily. But they watch completely different signals and protect completely different things, and TCP runs both of them, simultaneously, on every single connection, all the time.
9. Common Mistakes

The most common mistake is treating flow control and congestion control as basically the same idea, since both end up making a TCP sender slow down and both involve a window that can shrink. They are triggered by different signals and solve different problems, one entirely local to a single receiver, the other about a shared resource that no connection controls alone, and mixing them up leads to genuinely wrong explanations of why a connection slowed down.

A second, subtler mistake is assuming congestion is purely the network's problem to solve, something routers alone should handle, with individual connections just along for the ride. In reality, the internet has no central authority forcing anyone to slow down. It works specifically because every TCP connection voluntarily, cooperatively participates in avoiding congestion, backing off on its own the moment it detects trouble.
